title: Central Park (Stapleton)
name: Central Park (Stapleton)
metaDescription: Central Park 1031 exchange coordination for grocery-anchored retail and stabilized multifamily on the former Stapleton airport site, one of the metro's newest submarkets.

sections.html: Central Park is the old Stapleton airport, rebuilt from the runways up. Nearly everything trading here was built in the last two decades, which makes it one of the newest submarkets in the whole metro, and that newness changes how a seller should think about identification. The name change from Stapleton to Central Park is still recent enough that some title and permit records reference the old name, which a buyer's title company should reconcile early.

sections.heading: A Master Plan Instead of Organic Growth
sections.html: Where most Denver neighborhoods grew block by block over a century, Central Park was planned all at once after the airport closed and redeveloped in phases. That means the retail centers, apartment buildings, and mixed-use blocks here are more uniform in age and construction quality than almost anywhere else in the metro, which simplifies some diligence and complicates other parts of it, since uniform construction also means shared systemic issues show up in multiple buildings at once. The street grid itself was designed around the master plan rather than inherited from an older layout, which is worth knowing when comparing traffic patterns to an organically grown neighborhood nearby, since access points and visibility were engineered rather than accumulated over time.

sections.heading: What's Trading
sections.html:
Grocery-anchored retail centers built during the master plan's middle phases make up a steady share of exchange volume, particularly near Eastbridge Town Center. Newer multifamily communities built to the plan's density targets trade often as investors rotate in and out of stabilized assets. Some of the earliest-phase retail, now twenty years old, is starting to need repositioning. Newer phases toward the east side of the neighborhood are still being built out, which means a buyer should always confirm exactly which phase and delivery year a candidate belongs to rather than assuming the whole area shares one age profile, since even a five-year gap in delivery can mean meaningfully different construction standards and, occasionally, a different builder's warranty terms altogether. Categories worth tracking:

  • Grocery-anchored retail near Eastbridge Town Center
  • Stabilized multifamily built to the master plan's density targets
  • Early-phase retail approaching its first major repositioning cycle
  • Medical and service office serving the neighborhood's built-out population
  • DST interests for owners rotating out of direct multifamily ownership

sections.heading: The 95% Rule Fits a Uniform Market
sections.html: Because so much Central Park product was built to similar specifications around the same time, a seller here can often identify a long list of genuinely comparable candidates and use the 95% rule, naming more properties than the three-property rule allows and closing on nearly all of them, since the risk of a candidate falling through is lower in a market this consistent. That said, an investor should still confirm which phase each candidate was built in, since even a few years' difference in construction standards can matter.

sections.heading: Diligence on the Oldest Phases
sections.html: The earliest-built sections of Central Park are now old enough that roof, HVAC, and parking lot replacement cycles are starting to hit. A buyer looking at first-phase retail should ask directly which building systems are original and which have already been replaced, rather than assuming twenty-year-old construction is still under warranty. Reserve fund balances at any multifamily property here are worth checking closely for the same reason.

sections.heading: Coordinating a Straightforward Close
sections.html: Because the market here is newer and more standardized, closings tend to move faster than in older, more idiosyncratic Denver neighborhoods. That speed can work against a seller who hasn't lined up the qualified intermediary and lender early, since an active buyer pool doesn't wait for a seller who's still getting their paperwork in order. Getting documentation ready before the relinquished sale even closes pays off here more than in most submarkets, and I ask sellers to have their entity documents and prior surveys pulled before the clock even starts.

faqs.q: Why is the 95% rule a good fit for Central Park exchanges?
faqs.a: Product here was built to a master plan's consistent specifications, so a seller can often identify a longer list of genuinely comparable candidates with less risk of one falling through, which fits the 95% rule better than a thinner, more varied market. Still confirm each candidate's specific construction phase before finalizing anything.

faqs.q: What should I check on the earliest-phase Central Park retail?
faqs.a: Ask which major building systems, roof, HVAC, parking lot, are original and which have already been replaced. The oldest sections are now old enough that these replacement cycles are starting to hit, and reserve fund balances deserve the same scrutiny.

faqs.q: Is multifamily a common 1031 replacement in Central Park?
faqs.a: Yes. Stabilized multifamily built to the master plan's density targets trades regularly as investors rotate in and out of these assets, and comparable product is easier to find here than in older, less uniform neighborhoods.

faqs.q: Why do Central Park deals move faster than deals in older Denver neighborhoods?
faqs.a: The market is newer, more standardized, and draws an active buyer pool, so closings move quickly. A seller should have the qualified intermediary and lender lined up early rather than assuming extra time will be available before the 180-day deadline.

faqs.q: Can 1031 Exchange Denver tell me which Central Park property is the best investment?
faqs.a: No. This service coordinates identification logistics and communication with the investor's advisors. Which property best fits an investor's goals is a decision made with the investor's own broker and CPA.
